The system is designed for a small team whose schedules overlap only briefly, so each entry needs to be clear enough for someone who did not see the previous shift.

Staff check the surface and weight of representative pots, inspect the drainage trays, and compare their observations with the moisture notes recorded the day before. A dry-looking surface alone does not establish that a root ball needs water, particularly in the larger containers in Bay C. Conversely, seed trays in Bay A can dry quickly near the warm-air outlet, even when the surrounding benches feel cool. The person on duty records whether watering was needed, which bench was checked, and any unusual change in leaf color or growth. This gives the next shift a useful history without turning routine observations into diagnoses.

The regular rota runs from Monday through Saturday, with a shorter inspection on Sunday. The opening shift begins at 7:30 a.m. and checks the hose connections, water temperature, and the level in the rainwater tank before using the watering wand. The afternoon shift starts at 1:00 p.m. and reviews the morning notes before deciding whether a second check is necessary. Staff avoid watering leaves late in the day because damp foliage can remain wet overnight. When a scheduled check is postponed by deliveries or maintenance, the person responsible writes the revised time on the clipboard rather than leaving the next person to guess whether the task was completed.

1. **Bay A — propagation:** Check the moisture of the seed trays and plug cells at the front, center, and warm-air end of each bench. Use the narrow-spout can for small cells and apply water slowly, allowing it to soak in rather than run across the tray. If a tray is already evenly moist, record the check and do not water it again just to match another tray. Move any standing water from beneath the cells after the final check.
2. **Bay B — herbs and leafy crops:** Inspect one container from each bench and check the bed edges as well as the center. Water at soil level, taking care not to wash compost onto the walkway. The basil bench dries faster than the parsley bench on sunny days, but its condition still needs to be checked before watering. Mark any blocked drainage hole for the maintenance list.
3. **Bay C — fruiting plants:** Check the soil beside the stems without disturbing roots, and look for water in the saucers. If the hose coupling leaks, place the red tag on it and notify the shift lead before the next watering round. Do not leave a hose stretched across the central aisle, even when another person is expected to use it shortly afterward.

The thermometer beside Bay B is read at the start of both shifts, and the reading is written beside the date rather than in a separate notebook. If the overnight forecast is below 10°C, the closing shift checks that the vent levers are secured and tells the morning staff to assess the pots before opening the vents. This condition matters to the watering decision: cold, wet compost can remain saturated for longer, so the morning worker must rely on the pot checks and not assume that the usual early watering is appropriate. If the thermometer reading differs sharply from the forecast, the shift lead is informed and the discrepancy is recorded.

Several practical details help the rota work during busy periods. The rainwater tank usually supplies the greenhouse, while the mains tap is kept available if the tank level is too low for the planned round. Staff use the same clean, labeled hose for either source and note a change of supply on the clipboard. Fertilizer is not added as part of routine watering; any feeding is listed separately by the crop lead, with the date and mixture written down before it is prepared. A new worker should be shown how to read the jug marks and where to find the crop notes before being assigned a solo shift. The crop lead checks the clipboard each Wednesday and follows up on blank entries, repeated drainage problems, or observations that have not yet been addressed.

The handover is brief but specific. The outgoing worker points out any bench that was skipped, any plant that needs another moisture check, and any equipment issue that could affect the next shift. A note such as “Bay A, warm end: checked at 8:10; cells moist, no water added” is more useful than a general statement that propagation was finished. Staff use direct descriptions rather than guessing at causes: “lower leaves pale on two pepper plants” records what was seen, while a conclusion about the reason belongs to the crop lead after further inspection. If a job cannot be completed before the shift ends, the outgoing worker writes the reason, the remaining task, and the time it was last checked.

The clipboard also holds a monthly rota sheet that names the primary and backup workers for each day. The backup is responsible only when the primary worker is absent or asks for help, and the change is noted so two people do not unknowingly repeat the same round. On public holidays, the shift lead confirms the reduced staffing plan at least two days beforehand and assigns the Sunday-style inspection if the usual afternoon shift is not covered. Delivery days are marked on the sheet because pallets sometimes block access to the tank or the main aisle. In that case, staff check which route remains safe before carrying water, and they record any bay they could not reach rather than moving heavy loads alone.

At the end of each week, the crop lead reviews the records for patterns that may help adjust the rota, such as one bench drying faster after a change in ventilation or repeated standing water beneath a particular group of pots. These observations guide future checks but do not automatically change the watering plan. A change to the assigned times, equipment, or crop responsibilities is written on the rota and dated so everyone can see when it took effect. The current sheet remains posted until its replacement is ready, and older sheets are filed in the greenhouse office for reference. Keeping those records together makes it possible to understand what was checked, what was left for the next shift, and how the greenhouse routine changed through the season.", "output": "The propagation greenhouse at Alder Creek Farm uses a written watering rota to keep work consistent across its three growing bays.
